text.p: After almost 20 years of war, Afghanistan's sporting institutions are as devastated as the rest of the country.
But on Saturday morning, 120 men raced through the shattered heart of Kabul as part of a programme to revive sporting traditions.
They ran a 10,000-metre course from the shell of the once magnificent Darulaman Palace to the national stadium, a hulk of crumbling concrete pock-marked by bullets and shrapnel.

"Everything has been stolen from the stadium, so for the last two to three months we have been working with other agencies to rehabilitate it," said Greg Wilson of the United Nations' Habitat agency on Saturday morning.
"We have provided paint and plaster, roof sheets, doors and windows. The National Olympic Committee has provided all the labour," said Wilson, whose agency co-sponsored the run.
He said that two weeks ago 250 sportsmen turned up at the stadium as volunteers to help in the rebuilding.

"It needs a lot of work, but the roof is now weatherproof and German Agro Action (an aid agency) is in the process of replacing the doors and windows. The stadium is an important symbol," said Wilson, himself a keen sportsman.
As part of the rehabilitation programme, the stadium has been checked for mines and unexploded ammunition.
Outside the stadium on Saturday, mine awareness groups set up stalls as part of their campaign to raise awareness about land mines.
The de-mining agencies are currently running a mine action and awareness month to inform Afghans on the dangers of landmines and encourage the international campaign for banning landmines.
Afghanistan is one of the most heavily mined countries in the world. The United Nations estimates that up to 10 million mines have been laid during the Afghan conflict.
The Taleban have been keen to encourage sports in the 75 percent of Afghanistan they control, but insist that all sportsmen adhere to their purist interpretation of Islamic law.
Before the race the Taleban's religious police -- the Department for Promoting Virtue and Preventing Vice -- issued a set of guidelines for participants.

"The race should not conflict with prayer times and betting is forbidden. Runners' bodies should be properly covered, and arrogance and pride during the preceedings will be supressed," read a copy of the rules sent to Habitat. The runners, who were all men, had their arms and legs covered.

"The imitation of alien traditions, such as clapping and cheering while winning, is forbidden. It is only permissable to encourage sportsmen by shouting Allahu Akbar (God is Greatest), Sobhana Allah (praise be to God), and Alhamdu-lillah (thanks be to God)."
Thousands of Kabul's residents turned out to watch the race. Small boys who normally sell glasses of water from buckets doused the passing runners as temperatures rose above 30 degrees Celsius.
The winner won one million Afghanis ($45), a small cup, and a pair of plimsolls.
